I know I can trade profitably. I know what an edge looks like. The problem is how rare the truly clear trades are. Maybe 10 per year.

Then there are about 100 "not bad, not great" bets in between. In pure EV terms, taking them is correct if sizing is perfect.

But I am human. Greed, bad sizing, the urge to gamble. Almost all of my mistakes come from allowing myself to take those middle trades.

So what's left is at best 10 trades a year and long stretches of patient waiting. Being only a trader is not enough to fill the time in between.

tweets.text:
A says B lies. B says C lies. C says A and B both lie. Who tells the truth?

Stop here and think about it. What's your answer?

.

.

.

At first I thought it was impossible, that there had to be several valid answers. I felt stupid for a moment and said "probably C, but it could be any of them."

Then I asked my quant, a PhD in quantum physics with a 160+ IQ and several Millennium Prizes to his name. He said: "Try inverting the question, young one."

Ohhh. Forget who tells the truth. Who is lying? In what scenario do we get one truth and two lies?

If C is honest, then A and B both lie. But if A lies, B is telling the truth. Contradiction. C is a liar.

If A is honest, then B lies, which makes C honest. But C says A lies. Contradiction again. A is a liar.

That leaves B. If B is honest, C lies and A lies too. Everything fits. 

Trading works the same way. Instead of asking "why should I take this trade?", ask "why shouldn't I? What could go wrong? Should I cut it?"

I wrote about this years ago, then stopped practicing it. It's old wisdom, and it's as relevant as ever. 

It works at home too. If your wife asks "Should we go on a trip? Should we go shopping?", reply: "Should we stay home? Should we avoid materialism?" 

Invert the question. Often. Automatically.

$BTC Looking at all the previous bear market bottoms, after the first impulse you usually get a retrace of at least the .618 and often deeper. That is where we are now.

The 2018 and 2022 bottoms did take about 2 months to play out after the last leg down.

The 2020 covid crash resolved much faster but that also was a very unique situation.

Never have we seen a direct V shape without some kind of retest lower after the initial bounce. Even though zooming out might look like that, intraday/week we have had a retest every time. So this is normal.

For the sake of this example, assuming the 21st of November was the bottom (no one knows neither do I) we could also argue that this "bottoming" was already in process since June when price already hit this level. This cycle and bear market has been nothing like the others so it will be hard to take an example in that.

The point I wanted to make is that it is normal for these initial impulses to see a big drawdown. As I've seen a lot of mentions that the fact this didn't directly V shape back up and held above $62K was a case for the current low to not be valid. Even though we can see that has never been the case anyways. I agree, things look very weak relatively, but also that is normal for these situations.

In the end no one knows, maybe we get another leg down, maybe we do not. All I'm showing here is how previous major bottoms looked and that you always see a retrace that goes pretty deep.

Just for informational purposes, personally not sure what the next week(s) will bring us. Still believe anything around this region is solid high timeframe value for $BTC if you believe in it long term. Long road ahead of us though that's for sure.

WHY I THINK THIS BEAR MARKET IS DIFFERENT

I think one of the biggest mistakes people are making right now is trying to analyze this bear market through the lens of previous cycles.

The environment has fundamentally changed, and there are several bearish catalysts that deserve far more attention.

1. Bitcoin miners pivoting towards AI.

Some of the largest mining companies are diversifying into AI infrastructure and high-performance computing. Bitcoin mining is no longer their only opportunity to monetize energy and computing infrastructure.

2. Competition for capital.

Artificial intelligence, quantum computing, robotics, and other emerging technologies are competing for the speculative capital and attention that previously flowed into crypto.

Crypto is no longer the only exciting technological investment.

3. Narrative exhaustion.

ICOs, DeFi, NFTs, the metaverse, gaming, memecoins. The industry has burned through countless narratives without delivering enough sustainable value to justify the speculation.

4. Destruction of retail confidence.

Years of scams, insider enrichment, failed projects, and devastating losses have damaged the industry's reputation. Attracting fresh retail capital may become increasingly difficult.

5. Excessive token supply.

There are millions of tokens competing for liquidity. Add continuous token unlocks, emissions, and selling pressure from early investors, and you have a fundamentally challenging environment for altcoins.

6. The macroeconomic environment.

Bitcoin has never experienced a prolonged equity bear market comparable to 2000 or 2008. If the AI bubble bursts and traditional markets enter a sustained downturn, crypto could face an unprecedented macroeconomic stress test.

7. Institutional capital doesn't guarantee permanent demand.

ETFs have made Bitcoin more accessible, but they've also created another channel through which capital can leave during periods of risk aversion. Institutional adoption doesn't eliminate market cycles.

Individually, none of these factors necessarily guarantees a prolonged bear market. Collectively, however, they paint a concerning picture.

Yet people are still using historical cycle models to predict when the bottom will form, how deep the correction will be, and when the next altseason will begin.

Why assume the outcome will be the same when the underlying conditions are so different?

I don't believe crypto is going to disappear. I believe the industry needs a massive structural reset, and only a fraction of today's projects will emerge stronger from it.

In my opinion, this bear market will be remembered not only for the destruction of capital, but also for the destruction of confidence.

And confidence takes considerably longer to recover than price.

That's why I expect this bear market to be particularly painful, not just in terms of price, but also in terms of duration.

The real capitulation is still ahead of us.

BITCOIN: WHAT THE MONTHLY RSI IS TELLING US

One of the most interesting patterns in Bitcoin's history is how the monthly RSI has consistently formed lower lows at each major bear market bottom.

2011, 2015, 2018, 2022.

Every cycle has followed the same descending structure, with momentum reaching progressively lower levels during capitulation.

Currently, the monthly RSI is sitting around 42.7, while the historical structure suggests a potential bottom somewhere in the 30–35 region.

Now, looking at this chart, you might think we're relatively close to the bottom.

But here's where people need to be careful.

Being close to a bottom in terms of momentum doesn't necessarily mean we're close in terms of price.

The final stages of a bear market are often the most aggressive. A relatively small decline in the monthly RSI can accompany a substantial decline in Bitcoin's price.

This is typically when the remaining conviction disappears, long-term holders begin questioning their positions, and genuine capitulation takes place.

Of course, historical patterns are not guarantees, and the RSI should never be used in isolation.

However, this structure remains consistent with my broader bearish thesis.

I believe we're approaching the most psychologically challenging phase of this bear market, but we're not there yet.

Don't underestimate the amount of damage the market can do during its final leg down.

The last stretch is often the most brutal.

Patience.
